claim: Motor neurons of the crustacean cardiac ganglion generate virtually identical, synchronized output despite the fact that each neuron uses distinct conductance magnitudes.
source: Motor neurons of the crustacean cardiac ganglion generate virtually identical, synchronized output despite the fact that each neuron uses distinct conductance magnitudes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational observation about the cardiac ganglion system.

claim: Manipulations that target ionic conductances have distinct effects on neurons within the same ganglion, disrupting synchronized motor neuron output.
source: As a result of this variability, manipulations that target ionic conductances have distinct effects on neurons within the same ganglion, disrupting synchronized motor neuron output that is necessary for proper cardiac function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Blocking high-threshold K+ conductances in motor neurons within the ongoing cardiac network results in compensation that both resynchronizes the network and helps restore excitability.
source: By blocking high-threshold K+ conductances in motor neurons within the ongoing cardiac network, we discovered that compensation both resynchronized the network and helped restore excitability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Compensatory increases of both GA and electrical coupling restored function in the network.
source: Using model findings to guide experimentation, we determined that compensatory increases of both GA and electrical coupling restored function in the network.
evidence: This claim is supported by both modeling results (Figure 7) and experimental validation (Figures 4 and 6).

claim: This is one of the first direct demonstrations of the physiological regulation of coupling conductance in a compensatory context.
source: This is one of the first direct demonstrations of the physiological regulation of coupling conductance in a compensatory context, and of synergistic plasticity across cell- and network-level mechanisms in the restoration of output.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: Networks can exhibit a five-fold or more range in intrinsic and synaptic conductance values despite having nearly identical output across animals.
source: For instance, despite having nearly identical output across animals, networks can exhibit a five-fold or more range in intrinsic and synaptic conductance values (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Schulz et al., 2006; Marder, 2011; Roffman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Variability in intrinsic conductances has been documented in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: Such variability in intrinsic conductances is not limited to CPGs, but has been documented in several cell types of the mammalian brain, including cerebellar Purkinje cells (Swensen and Bean, 2005), and globus pallidus neurons (Günay et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swensen and Bean, 2005.

claim: Variability in intrinsic conductances has been documented in globus pallidus neurons.
source: Such variability in intrinsic conductances is not limited to CPGs, but has been documented in several cell types of the mammalian brain, including cerebellar Purkinje cells (Swensen and Bean, 2005), and globus pallidus neurons (Günay et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Günay et al., 2008.

claim: Synaptic strengths between mammalian central neurons vary in several brain regions.
source: Additionally, the synaptic strengths between mammalian central neurons have been shown to vary in several brain regions (Nelson and Turrigiano, 2008; Turrigiano, 2008; Maffei et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Five Large Cell motor neurons (LCs) in the cardiac ganglion of Cancer borealis generate completely synchronous output.
source: In the cardiac ganglion (CG) of the Jonah crab (Cancer borealis), five Large Cell motor neurons (LCs) generate completely synchronous output, as a result of pacemaker inputs within the network, to drive simultaneous heart muscle contraction in the crab (Tazaki, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tazaki, 1972.

claim: LCs show highly variable underlying maximal conductances despite completely uniform and synchronous activity.
source: Despite completely uniform and synchronous activity within the network, LCs show highly variable underlying maximal conductances (Ransdell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2012.

claim: When high-threshold K+ currents were blocked with TEA, motor neurons lost coordinated output and became divergent in their patterns of firing.
source: These variable conductances render the neurons susceptible to perturbations that target a subset of ionic conductances: when high-threshold K+ currents were blocked with tetraethylammonium (TEA), the motor neurons lost coordinated output and became divergent in their patterns of firing (Ransdell et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2013a.

claim: 25 mM TEA reduces the magnitude of high-threshold K+ currents (IKd + IBKKCA) by ~92% in isolated LCs.
source: Ransdell et al. (2013a) were able to repeatably reduce the magnitude of high-threshold K+ currents (IKd + IBKKCA) by ~92% in isolated LCs with 25 mM TEA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2013a and describes a specific experimental result.

claim: After application of TEA, motor neurons became noticeably more depolarized during burst potentials and LC spiking increased substantially.
source: After application of TEA, motor neurons became noticeably more depolarized during burst potentials and LC spiking seen on the extracellular recordings increased substantially (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Comparison of intracellular voltage waveforms revealed a loss of conserved output after TEA exposure.
source: Additionally, comparison of intracellular voltage waveforms revealed a loss of conserved output (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Acutely after application of TEA, there was a significant reduction in synchrony as measured by R2 across LC voltage waveforms.
source: Acutely after application of TEA, we saw a significant reduction in synchrony as measured by R2 (see Materials and methods; Ransdell et al., 2013a) across LC voltage waveforms (Figure 2B,C, time point II).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Waveform synchrony values consistently recovered towards baseline levels, often by 30 min, and were no longer statistically different from baseline by 1 hr of treatment with TEA.
source: Following this reduction, waveform synchrony values consistently recovered towards baseline levels, often by 30 min, and were no longer statistically different from baseline by 1 hr of treatment with TEA (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Spikes per burst, average spike frequency, total burst depolarization and burst amplitude all were significantly increased immediately after exposure to TEA.
source: The spikes per burst, average spike frequency, total burst depolarization and burst amplitude all were significantly increased immediately after exposure to TEA ('acute'), while the small cell pacemaker (SC)-to-LC phase delay was significantly decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The SC-to-LC phase delay was significantly decreased immediately after exposure to TEA.
source: The spikes per burst, average spike frequency, total burst depolarization and burst amplitude all were significantly increased immediately after exposure to TEA ('acute'), while the small cell pacemaker (SC)-to-LC phase delay was significantly decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All 5 measures of excitability showed a significant change back towards their baseline levels between the 30 min and 60 min time points.
source: All 5 measures also then showed a significant change back towards their baseline levels between the 30 min and 60 min time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The SC-LC phase delay was fully restored after 60 minutes of TEA exposure.
source: While all measures showed clear shifts towards restoration of baseline excitability, the number of spikes per burst, spike frequency within each burst, burst amplitude, and total burst depolarization were not completely restored to control levels; the exception was the SC-LC phase delay which was fully restored (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A population of 27 model CG networks with variable underlying conductances successfully recapitulated the biological data observed in TEA.
source: Our model development and selection criteria resulted in a population of 27 model CG networks with variable underlying conductances of the constituent neurons that successfully recapitulated the biological data observed in TEA (see Methods, Supplemental Information).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling methodology described in the Methods section.

claim: Previous results identified an approximate 2.2 ± 0.8-fold change in IA in LCs as a result of 60 min of TEA exposure.
source: Our previous results identified an approximate 2.2 ± 0.8-fold change in IA in LCs as a result of 60 min of TEA exposure (Ransdell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ransdell et al., 2012.

claim: Two-fold increase in GA resulted in a mean synchrony score that was significantly different from the TEA case but not significantly different from control.
source: The optimal solution of significantly improving spike synchrony and also significantly decreasing the total number of action potentials was achieved in only one case: two-fold increase in GA resulted in a mean synchrony score that was significantly different from the TEA case (p<0.05, paired t-test) but not significantly different from control (p=0.157).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: No other change in a given conductance resulted in the combination of improved synchrony and decreased action potentials.
source: No other change in a given conductance resulted in this combination of statistical outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A given ratio range (~1:0.83 respectively) of ICAN to ISKKCa was necessary for proper termination of the activity.
source: Subsequent trials revealed that a given ratio range (~1:0.83 respectively) of these two currents was necessary for proper termination of the activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results described in the Methods section.

claim: The model demonstrates that waveform synchrony can translate into spike synchrony.
source: Importantly, the model also extends the biological data by demonstrating that waveform synchrony can translate into spike synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The initial voltage responses to stimulation protocol in LC3 and LC5 in control conditions are highly similar to one another.
source: The initial voltage responses to our stimulation protocol in LC3 and LC5 in control conditions are highly similar to one another, and their level of waveform synchrony was not significantly different from the synchronous activity across these LCs during intact control network activity (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Immediately following TEA application, LC3 and LC5 show disparate output when driven with a common stimulus protocol.
source: Immediately following TEA application, LC3 and LC5 show disparate output when driven with a common stimulus protocol (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There were significant increases in R2 of voltage activity within 1 hr across isolated LCs.
source: Finally, our data show significant increases in R2 of voltage activity within 1 hr across isolated LCs (Figure 4B), demonstrating that intrinsic compensation does improve network synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After 1 hr the synchrony values were significantly lower than control values, suggesting that intrinsic compensation alone is insufficient to restore synchrony.
source: However, after 1 hr the synchrony values were significantly lower than control values (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that intrinsic compensation alone is insufficient to restore synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C and statistical analysis.

claim: In all cases peak IA current increased after 1 hr of TEA exposure, with a mean increase of 56%.
source: In all cases peak IA current increased (Figure 4D), with a mean increase of 56% (p<0.05, n = 6, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental voltage clamp data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The voltage response after compensation was significantly different from the control voltage response, indicating that intrinsic compensation does not restore the original cellular output.
source: However, the voltage response after compensation was significantly different from the control voltage response (p<0.01, n = 8, Wilcoxon signed rank test), indicating that intrinsic compensation does not restore the original cellular output (Figure 4E; control vs. TEA [1 Hour]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and statistical analysis.

claim: Increasing the strength of either chemical synapses or electrical coupling increased both synchrony and excitability in model networks.
source: We found that increasing the strength of either chemical synapses or electrical coupling increased both synchrony and excitability (Figure 5 left).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Increasing the chemical synaptic conductance in conjunction with TEA blockade increases spiking of the LCs ~25–30% in contrast to the biological decrease in excitability.
source: However, increasing the chemical synaptic conductance in conjunction with TEA blockade also increases spiking of the LCs ~25–30% in contrast to the biological decrease in excitability relative to the acute TEA exposure seen with compensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Only a small change in LC spiking occurs with an increase in electrical coupling (~9%).
source: Conversely, only a small change in LC spiking occurs with an increase in electrical coupling (~9%, Figure 5 left).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Reducing the strength of either chemical synapses or electrical coupling decreased overall spike synchrony.
source: Reducing the strength of either chemical synapses or electrical coupling decreased overall spike synchrony (Figure 5 right), violating the assumptions of compensation based on the biological data.
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Increasing the artificial coupling conductance significantly increased the correlation coefficient of the waveform between two cells.
source: Increasing the artificial coupling conductance significantly increased the correlation coefficient of the waveform between the two cells (Figure 6A), with a synaptic conductance value of 0.2 μS able to rescue synchrony of LCs to levels observed in intact networks (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using dynamic clamp shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Coupling coefficient between LCs increased significantly after 1 hr in TEA (mean increase 85%).
source: Coupling coefficients between cells increased significantly after 1 hr in TEA (mean increase 85%, p<0.01; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the apparent input resistance of LCs in control physiological saline, after acute TEA exposure, or after compensation.
source: Using two-electrode current clamp, we saw no significant differences in the apparent input resistance of LCs in control physiological saline, after acute TEA exposure, or after compensation (1 hr TEA exposure; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Changes in passive membrane conductance (GLeak) are not responsible for increased coupling coefficients.
source: These results indicate that changes in passive membrane conductance (GLeak) are not responsible for increased coupling coefficients.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that input resistance did not change.

claim: Coupling conductance (GC) between LC4 and LC5 significantly increased during 1 hr of TEA exposure (mean increase 49.5%).
source: Coupling conductance (GC) between LC4 and LC5 significantly increased during 1 hr of TEA exposure (mean increase 49.5%, p<0.01, N = 8; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Increasing GA up to +40% promoted greater synchrony after TEA blockade, but was unable to fully restore synchrony even with increasing conductance levels.
source: Increasing GA up to +40% promoted greater synchrony after TEA blockade, but was unable to fully restore synchrony even with increasing conductance levels, consistent with our biological data (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Electrical coupling alone was capable of restoring synchrony fully, but this required a 140% increase in its value.
source: We also increased model GC incrementally (from +10% to +150%), and found that electrical coupling alone was capable of restoring synchrony fully, but this required a 140% increase in its value (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A smaller increase of 70% in each conductance (GA and GC) was able to produce spike synchrony that was indistinguishable from control.
source: Finally, we increased both GA and GC together in 10% increments, revealing a potentially synergistic relationship: a smaller increase of 70% in each conductance was able to produce spike synchrony that was indistinguishable from control (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 7.

claim: This is the first demonstration of coordinated homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic and electrical synaptic conductances in a comprehensive network-level example of homeostatic compensation.
source: While membrane conductances and properties of electrical coupling are known to interact in critically important ways to promote synchrony (Curti et al., 2012; Gutierrez and Marder, 2013), to our knowledge the present study is the first demonstration of coordinated homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic and electrical synaptic conductances in a comprehensive network-level example of homeostatic compensation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: K+ currents can increase or help restore synchrony between electrically coupled neurons.
source: Previous modelling studies found that K+ currents can increase or help restore synchrony between electrically coupled neurons (Pfeuty et al., 2003), so we first hypothesized that a compensatory increase in A-Type K+ membrane conductance could be a mechanism underlying both restored excitability and resynchronization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pfeuty et al., 2003.

claim: Multi-component mechanisms are necessary for full compensation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that multi-component mechanisms are not only necessary for full compensation, but also that their synergistic action is potentially more efficient than either mechanism operating in isolation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the modeling and experimental results showing that combined changes in GA and GC are more effective than either alone.

claim: Chaotic exploratory and consummatory radula biting movements of Aplysia during food searching behaviour can be stably modified by operant conditioning.
source: In a series of elegant experiments, it has been shown that chaotic exploratory and consummatory radula biting movements of Aplysia during food searching behaviour can be stably modified by operant conditioning, leading to prolonged bouts of radula movements with increased frequency and more stereotyped rhythmic organization (Nargeot et al., 2007; Nargeot and Simmers, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nargeot et al., 2007 and Nargeot and Simmers, 2011.

claim: In Aplysia, changes in intrinsic excitability attributed to changes in leak conductance underlie the increase in frequency of motor output.
source: Specifically, changes in intrinsic excitability attributed to changes in leak conductance underlie the increase in frequency of motor output, while increases in coupling strength allow for the synchronization and regularization of bursting (Nargeot et al., 2009; Sieling et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nargeot et al., 2009 and Sieling et al., 2014.

claim: In Aplysia, increases in coupling strength allow for the synchronization and regularization of bursting.
source: Specifically, changes in intrinsic excitability attributed to changes in leak conductance underlie the increase in frequency of motor output, while increases in coupling strength allow for the synchronization and regularization of bursting (Nargeot et al., 2009; Sieling et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nargeot et al., 2009 and Sieling et al., 2014.

claim: Electrical coupling has long been known to promote synchrony in many systems, including the CG.
source: Although electrical coupling has long been known to promote synchrony in many systems, including the CG (Tazaki, 1972; Bennett and Zukin, 2004), the physiological interaction of electrical coupling with intrinsic conductances to affect a compensatory output has not been examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tazaki, 1972 and Bennett and Zukin, 2004.

claim: The synchronized activity of pacemaker cells in the crustacean STG is dependent on an interaction of intrinsic conductances and electrical coupling.
source: Previous work in the crustacean STG has demonstrated how the synchronized activity of pacemaker cells is dependent on an interaction of intrinsic conductances and electrical coupling (Szücs et al., 2000, 2001; Soto-Treviño et al., 2005), and that distinct circuits can be brought into synchrony via manipulations of electrical and chemical synapses (Elson et al., 1998; Szücs et al., 2000, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on the STG.

claim: Plasticity of electrical synapses has been discovered in the mammalian central nervous system, including the thalamic reticular nucleus.
source: Similarly, plasticity of electrical synapses has drawn considerable attention after being discovered in the mammalian central nervous system, including the thalamic reticular nucleus (Landisman and Connors, 2005; Haas et al., 2011), inferior olive (Lefler et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2014), and retina (Kothmann et al., 2009; Völgyi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Landisman and Connors, 2005 and Haas et al., 2011.

claim: Plasticity of electrical synapses has been discovered in the mammalian inferior olive.
source: Similarly, plasticity of electrical synapses has drawn considerable attention after being discovered in the mammalian central nervous system, including the thalamic reticular nucleus (Landisman and Connors, 2005; Haas et al., 2011), inferior olive (Lefler et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2014), and retina (Kothmann et al., 2009; Völgyi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lefler et al., 2014 and Mathy et al., 2014.

claim: Plasticity of electrical synapses has been discovered in the mammalian retina.
source: Similarly, plasticity of electrical synapses has drawn considerable attention after being discovered in the mammalian central nervous system, including the thalamic reticular nucleus (Landisman and Connors, 2005; Haas et al., 2011), inferior olive (Lefler et al., 2014; Mathy et al., 2014), and retina (Kothmann et al., 2009; Völgyi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kothmann et al., 2009 and Völgyi et al., 2013.

claim: Studies in the thalamic reticular nucleus have suggested that potentially compensatory changes in coupling are important to maintain network stability as large changes in intrinsic excitability occur across development.
source: Studies in the thalamic reticular nucleus have suggested that potentially compensatory changes in coupling are important to maintain network stability as large changes in intrinsic excitability occur across development (Parker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parker et al., 2009.

claim: Intrinsic conductances can be differentially affected by neuromodulation.
source: Intrinsic conductances can be differentially affected by ubiquitous natural mechanisms such as neuromodulation (Marder, 2011, 2012) or temperature changes (Tang et al., 2012; Marder et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marder, 2011, 2012.

claim: Intrinsic conductances can be differentially affected by temperature changes.
source: Intrinsic conductances can be differentially affected by ubiquitous natural mechanisms such as neuromodulation (Marder, 2011, 2012) or temperature changes (Tang et al., 2012; Marder et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2012 and Marder et al., 2015.

claim: The effectiveness of electrical coupling can be affected by the modulation of intrinsic cellular conductances.
source: Further, the effectiveness of electrical coupling can be affected by the modulation of intrinsic cellular conductances (Szabo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szabo et al., 2010.

claim: The cardiac ganglion network is comprised of 9 cells: 4 Small Cell (SC) pacemaker interneurons which give simultaneous excitatory input to 5 Large Cell (LC) motor neurons.
source: The CG network is comprised of 9 cells: 4 Small Cell (SC) pacemaker interneurons which give simultaneous excitatory input to 5 Large Cell (LC) motor neurons.
evidence: This is a description of the network architecture based on established knowledge.

claim: Anterior LCs exhibit strong local electrical and dye coupling in the crab CG.
source: In the crab CG, anterior LCs exhibit strong local electrical and dye coupling (Tazaki and Cooke, 1979, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tazaki and Cooke, 1979, 1983.

claim: The model LC neurons consist of two compartments - soma and axon.
source: LC model neurons consist of two compartments - soma and axon - of which only the somata are pictured.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Somata in the model contain 9 conductances: GCaS, GCaT, GLEAK, GCAN, GA, GBKKCa, GSKKCa, GKd, and GNaP.
source: Somata contain 9 conductances: GCaS, GCaT, GLEAK, GCAN, GA, GBKKCa, GSKKCa, GKd, and GNaP.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Paired LCs (1+2, 4+5) have stronger local coupling in the model.
source: Paired LCs (1+2, 4+5) have stronger local coupling (black resistor symbols), and all 5 LCs are reciprocally electrically coupled via weaker gap junctions (gray resistor symbols).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All 5 LCs are reciprocally electrically coupled via weaker gap junctions in the model.
source: Paired LCs (1+2, 4+5) have stronger local coupling (black resistor symbols), and all 5 LCs are reciprocally electrically coupled via weaker gap junctions (gray resistor symbols).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Model networks exhibited 'control' synchrony scores ranging from 0.642 to 1.0 with a median value of 0.915.
source: Using the definition of synchrony listed in the next section, these randomly generated model networks exhibited 'control' synchrony scores ranging from 0.642 to 1.0 with a median value of 0.915 (matching data in biology), where 1.0 represents perfect spike synchrony.
evidence: This is a description of the model validation results.

claim: Because of the electrotonic distance between the somata and axons of LCs, spike synchrony cannot be measured directly in this preparation.
source: Because of the electrotonic distance between the somata and axons of LCs, we cannot measure spike synchrony directly in this preparation.
evidence: This is a statement about a technical limitation of the biological preparation.

claim: The model allows inference that waveform synchrony (and loss of synchrony) can translate to the level of the most proximal cellular output – spiking.
source: The model allows us to infer that waveform synchrony (and loss of synchrony) can indeed translate to the level of the most proximal cellular output – spiking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity has been reported in single isolated neurons.
source: Homeostatic plasticity has been reported in single isolated neurons (Swensen and Bean, 2005; Ransdell et al., 2012), in artificial networks formed in culture (Desai et al., 1999; Ibata et al., 2008), or in thin sections of the CNS (Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity has been reported in artificial networks formed in culture.
source: Homeostatic plasticity has been reported in single isolated neurons (Swensen and Bean, 2005; Ransdell et al., 2012), in artificial networks formed in culture (Desai et al., 1999; Ibata et al., 2008), or in thin sections of the CNS (Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Desai et al., 1999 and Ibata et al., 2008.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity has been reported in thin sections of the CNS.
source: Homeostatic plasticity has been reported in single isolated neurons (Swensen and Bean, 2005; Ransdell et al., 2012), in artificial networks formed in culture (Desai et al., 1999; Ibata et al., 2008), or in thin sections of the CNS (Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006 and Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013.

claim: Cortical slice preparations have demonstrated homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic conductances coordinated with chemical synaptic plasticity.
source: Cortical slice preparations have demonstrated homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic conductances coordinated with chemical synaptic plasticity (Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013), and Mauthner cells in fish have been shown to exhibit coordinated activity-dependent changes in both the chemical and electrical components of its mixed synapses (Yang et al., 1990; Pereda and Faber, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006 and Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013.

claim: Mauthner cells in fish have been shown to exhibit coordinated activity-dependent changes in both the chemical and electrical components of its mixed synapses.
source: Cortical slice preparations have demonstrated homeostatic plasticity of intrinsic conductances coordinated with chemical synaptic plasticity (Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013), and Mauthner cells in fish have been shown to exhibit coordinated activity-dependent changes in both the chemical and electrical components of its mixed synapses (Yang et al., 1990; Pereda and Faber, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 1990 and Pereda and Faber, 1996.

claim: Variability in underlying cellular parameters may form part of the repertoire of compensatory mechanisms that endow networks with remarkable robustness characteristics.
source: Moreover, only recently has there been an appreciation that variability in underlying cellular parameters such as conductance magnitudes (Schulz et al., 2006; Pratt and Aizenman, 2007; Wilhelm et al., 2009), activation properties of channels (Olypher et al., 2006; Amendola et al., 2012), and synaptic strengths (Olypher and Calabrese, 2007; Wilhelm et al., 2009; Grashow et al., 2010) may form part of the repertoire of compensatory mechanisms that endow networks with remarkable robustness characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and represents an interpretation of the literature.

claim: Degeneracy of ion channel properties has been put forth as a mechanism underlying robustness and adaptability in neural networks.
source: Degeneracy of ion channel properties leading to this type of relationship has been put forth as a mechanism underlying robustness and adaptability in neural networks (Tononi et al., 1999; Marder and Goaillard, 2006), but our study suggests physiological limits to neural network compensation and robustness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tononi et al., 1999 and Marder and Goaillard, 2006.

claim: The study suggests physiological limits to neural network compensation and robustness.
source: Degeneracy of ion channel properties leading to this type of relationship has been put forth as a mechanism underlying robustness and adaptability in neural networks (Tononi et al., 1999; Marder and Goaillard, 2006), but our study suggests physiological limits to neural network compensation and robustness.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that compensated LCs never recapitulated their original voltage waveforms.

claim: These limits may themselves be a contributing factor to the nature and progression of pathology in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: These limits may themselves be a contributing factor to the nature and progression of pathology in neurodegenerative diseases (Trasande and Ramirez, 2007; Beck and Yaari, 2008; Small, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to studies on neurodegenerative diseases.
